name: Product Management Fundamentals
description: Product vision and strategy, user research, problem framing, discovery and delivery, requirements, prioritisation, roadmaps, MVPs and experiments, product metrics, pricing, onboarding and launch, feedback loops, product-market fit, lifecycle and B2B, B2C and platform contexts for people who build or run products.

cards.subject: Product vision
says: describes the future the product is meant to create for its users
stays stable across several planning cycles
gives a team a shared reason for the product to exist
cards.use: need to explain why the product exists to a new team member
not: lists the features planned for next quarter

cards.subject: Product strategy
says: sets the choices about where to play and how to win
states which customers and problems the team will deliberately not serve
connects the vision to a coherent set of bets
cards.use: need to decide which of two promising opportunities to refuse
not: is a list of every feature in the backlog

cards.subject: Product principles
says: act as agreed rules that settle recurring trade-offs without escalation
describe what the team values when two good options collide
are specific enough that a reasonable team could disagree with them
cards.use: find teams re-arguing the same trade-off in every planning meeting
not: describe the target market size

cards.subject: Strategic bet
says: commits scarce capacity to an outcome that may not pay off
is written as a belief with a way of finding out it was wrong
accepts an opportunity cost in exchange for a possible large gain
cards.use: need to place a large investment under real uncertainty
not: is a guaranteed outcome with a fixed delivery date

cards.subject: Positioning statement
says: names the target customer, the category and the main benefit over alternatives
tells customers why this product is different from the next best option
is shared by product, marketing and sales
cards.use: hear sales and marketing describe the product in three different ways
not: is the legal description of the product in the terms of service

cards.subject: Competitive moat
says: makes a product costly for rivals to copy or for customers to leave
can come from network effects, switching costs, data or scale
erodes if the company stops investing in what created it
cards.use: are asked what protects the product once a larger rival copies the features
not: is any feature that a competitor has not yet built

cards.subject: Product-led growth
says: lets users reach value through the product itself before talking to sales
relies on onboarding, free tiers or trials to drive acquisition and expansion
treats the product as the main driver of conversion
cards.use: want users to try and adopt the product without a sales conversation
not: depends on a large outbound sales team to close every deal

cards.subject: Sales-led growth
says: relies on a sales team to find, demo and close customers
suits products with high contract values and complex buying processes
uses the sales conversation to shape deals that the product alone cannot close
cards.use: sell a high-value product that needs a long evaluation by several buyers
not: depends on users upgrading themselves without any contact

cards.subject: Opportunity cost
says: is the value of the best option given up when another is chosen
makes every yes to a feature a no to something else
applies even when the chosen work is profitable
cards.use: need to compare a proposed project with what the team would otherwise do
not: is the money paid to the vendors that build a feature

cards.subject: User interview
says: asks one person open questions about their past behaviour
uncovers motivations and context that numbers cannot show
works best when the interviewer listens more than talks
cards.use: want to learn why customers behave as they do
not: proves how many customers share a view

cards.subject: Contextual inquiry
says: observes users doing real work in their own environment
reveals workarounds that users forget to mention in interviews
combines watching with short questions in the moment
cards.use: suspect users have workarounds they will not describe
not: is a remote survey sent to a large panel

cards.subject: Survey
says: collects structured answers from many respondents at low cost
measures how common an attitude or behaviour is
is weak at explaining the reasons behind answers
cards.use: need to size how widespread a problem is across the customer base
not: uncovers unexpected needs through follow-up questions

cards.subject: Usability test
says: watches representative users try to complete realistic tasks
finds where the interface confuses people
can use a prototype long before engineering starts
cards.use: want to find where users get stuck in a flow before building it
not: measures the long-term retention of the feature

cards.subject: Diary study
says: asks participants to log experiences over days or weeks
captures behaviour that happens over time rather than in one session
costs participants effort, so dropout is a risk
cards.use: need to understand a habit that unfolds over several weeks
not: tests one prototype task in a single sitting

cards.subject: Card sorting
says: asks users to group items into categories they find natural
informs navigation and information architecture
reveals the labels people expect for content
cards.use: need to decide how to organise a menu with many items
not: measures task completion time on a checkout form

cards.subject: Affinity mapping
says: groups research notes by similarity to reveal themes
turns raw observations from many sessions into patterns
is done collaboratively so the whole team shares the findings
cards.use: have a pile of notes from a dozen interviews and need the main themes
not: scores features by reach and effort

cards.subject: Leading question
says: hints at the answer the interviewer hopes to hear
biases the response toward agreement
is avoided by asking about past behaviour openly
cards.use: review an interview script containing the phrase 'Wouldn't you love a dashboard for this?'
not: is an open question that lets the user choose the topic

cards.subject: Say-do gap
says: is the difference between what users claim and what they actually do
makes stated intentions a weak forecast of behaviour
is why observed behaviour outweighs opinion in research
cards.use: hear users say they would pay for a feature but usage data shows they ignore similar ones
not: is the delay between a bug report and its fix

cards.subject: Persona
says: is a research-based archetype of a group of users
summarises goals, context and pain points of a segment
goes stale if it is not refreshed with new research
cards.use: need a shared picture of the typical user across the team
not: is a single real customer named in a case study

cards.subject: Jobs to be done
says: frames what progress a customer is trying to make in a situation
looks at the circumstance and motivation rather than demographics
explains why customers switch from one solution to another
cards.use: find that customers with very different demographics hire the product for the same reason
not: groups users by age and job title

cards.subject: Job story
says: is written as a situation, a motivation and an expected outcome
drops the persona role and focuses on context
rewrites a user story around circumstance
cards.use: want a story format that describes the trigger instead of a type of user
not: begins with 'As a' and a named role

cards.subject: Problem statement
says: describes who has a problem, what it is and why it matters
is written without naming a solution
keeps a team solving the right thing before design starts
cards.use: find a team already debating button placement before agreeing what problem they solve
not: names the feature to be built and its release date

cards.subject: Opportunity solution tree
says: links a desired outcome to opportunities and then to candidate solutions
shows several solutions per opportunity instead of one
connects each experiment to the opportunity it tests
cards.use: want to show how experiments trace back to an outcome
not: lists tasks in a project plan by owner

cards.subject: Customer journey map
says: lays out the stages a customer goes through from awareness to use
marks emotions and pain points at each stage
exposes handoffs where the experience breaks
cards.use: need to find where the experience breaks between marketing, sign-up and first use
not: ranks features by estimated revenue

cards.subject: Customer segment
says: is a group of customers with shared needs or behaviour
lets the team decide whom to serve first
can be defined by behaviour as well as company traits
cards.use: need to choose which group of customers to focus a release on
not: is a named fictional character with a photo

cards.subject: Ideal customer profile
says: describes the kind of account that gets the most value and is most likely to succeed
guides sales, marketing and product focus together
is built from existing best customers, not wishes
cards.use: want sales to stop closing customers who churn within months
not: describes one user's day inside the product

cards.subject: Desired outcome
says: states a change in customer or business behaviour the team wants
is measurable and independent of any solution
turns a vague goal into something a team can test against
cards.use: want a team to aim at a result rather than a deliverable
not: is the list of features a stakeholder requested

cards.subject: Product discovery
says: decides what is worth building by testing ideas with users
reduces risk before engineering commits
continues alongside delivery rather than ending at a gate
cards.use: need evidence an idea is valuable before engineering builds it
not: builds and ships the agreed solution at quality

cards.subject: Product delivery
says: builds, tests and ships the chosen solution reliably
turns validated decisions into working software
is judged on quality, predictability and release cadence
cards.use: need to turn a validated design into production software
not: tests which problems customers care about

cards.subject: Dual-track agile
says: runs discovery and delivery in parallel by the same team
feeds validated work into the delivery backlog
avoids a hand-off between a research phase and a build phase
cards.use: want discovery and delivery to happen side by side instead of one after another
not: is a waterfall plan with a requirements gate

cards.subject: Product trio
says: pairs a product manager, a designer and an engineer in discovery
brings feasibility and usability into decisions early
shares customer contact across all three disciplines
cards.use: want engineering and design to join customer conversations from the start
not: is a committee of three executives that approves releases

cards.subject: Assumption mapping
says: lists what must be true for an idea to work and sorts it by risk and evidence
exposes the assumptions most likely to sink the idea
chooses the next test by the least evidence and the highest impact
cards.use: need to choose what to test first among dozens of unknowns
not: scores features by reach and effort

cards.subject: Riskiest assumption test
says: tests the belief that would most damage the idea if wrong
is cheaper than building the product to learn the same thing
is chosen before smaller, safer questions
cards.use: need the cheapest way to learn whether the whole idea can work
not: validates the easiest assumption first

cards.subject: Four product risks
says: cover value, usability, feasibility and business viability
divide discovery questions among product, design and engineering
remind a team that a buildable idea can still be unwanted
cards.use: find a team that proved an idea was feasible but never tested whether anyone wants it
not: are schedule, cost, scope and quality

cards.subject: Prototype
says: is a cheap simulation of an idea used to learn before building
can be a clickable mock or a paper sketch
is thrown away or rebuilt rather than shipped
cards.use: want user reactions to an interface before any code exists
not: is the production release candidate

cards.subject: Design sprint
says: compresses problem framing, ideas, prototype and user test into a few days
commits a small cross-functional team to one hard question
ends with real user reactions to a prototype
cards.use: need a fast, focused answer to a big, uncertain question with a cross-functional team
not: is a regular two-week delivery iteration

cards.subject: User story
says: describes a need from a user's point of view in a short sentence
invites a conversation rather than replacing it
fits into a single iteration when well sized
cards.use: need to describe a small piece of value from the user's side
not: is a full specification with every screen defined

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: state the conditions that must be met for a story to be accepted
are testable, with a clear pass or fail
are agreed before development starts
cards.use: need to know when a story is truly finished from the customer's view
not: describe how many engineers will work on a story

cards.subject: INVEST
says: lists the qualities of a good story: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable
gives a team a quick check on story quality
flags stories too large to estimate or test
cards.use: want a quick checklist to judge whether stories are well formed
not: scores features by reach and impact

cards.subject: Epic
says: is a large body of work that is split into stories
spans several iterations
groups stories under one larger goal
cards.use: have a goal too large to finish in one iteration
not: is a task that fits in one afternoon

cards.subject: Story splitting
says: breaks a large story into smaller ones that each deliver value
slices vertically through the whole flow rather than by layer
keeps each slice releasable on its own
cards.use: find a story too large for one iteration
not: divides work into separate database and interface tasks

cards.subject: Definition of done
says: is the team-wide quality bar every item must meet to be complete
covers tests, review and documentation for all stories
applies to every item, unlike per-story criteria
cards.use: find stories marked complete that still lack tests and review
not: lists the conditions for one story's acceptance

cards.subject: Definition of ready
says: is a checklist that a story must meet before the team starts it
covers clarity, size and dependencies known
can turn into a gate that slows the team if over-applied
cards.use: find a team pulling in stories that nobody understands
not: is the quality bar for completed work

cards.subject: Non-functional requirement
says: describes how well the system must work, such as speed, security or availability
is easy to forget in a story focused on features
often has a large effect on cost and architecture
cards.use: notice stories describe features but say nothing about speed or privacy
not: describes what a feature does for a user task

cards.subject: Given-When-Then
says: writes a scenario as a starting state, an action and an expected result
makes acceptance criteria readable by non-engineers and testable
gives a team one shared example per behaviour
cards.use: want acceptance criteria written as concrete scenarios
not: is a template for describing a persona

cards.subject: Product requirements document
says: records the problem, goals, scope and requirements for a release
is most useful when it captures the why and not only the what
stays lean and is updated as the team learns
cards.use: need one place that records the problem, scope and non-goals for a larger initiative
not: replaces all conversation between product and engineering

cards.subject: RICE
says: scores ideas by reach, impact, confidence and effort
divides reach times impact times confidence by effort
penalises ideas with weak evidence through the confidence factor
cards.use: need a numeric ranking that accounts for how sure the team is
not: sorts requests into must, should, could and won't

cards.subject: ICE
says: scores ideas on impact, confidence and ease
is faster than RICE because it has no reach estimate
suits quick growth experiments
cards.use: need a quick score for many experiment ideas without estimating reach
not: multiplies reach by impact over effort

cards.subject: MoSCoW
says: sorts requirements into must, should, could and won't have
forces a release to name what it will not include
is used to set scope within a fixed time or budget
cards.use: have a fixed deadline and need to agree what must be in the release
not: gives each idea a numeric score

cards.subject: Kano model
says: classifies features as basic, performance or delight
shows that delighters become expected over time
uses paired survey questions on having and lacking a feature
cards.use: want to know which features customers merely expect and which would delight
not: scores features by effort and reach

cards.subject: Value versus effort
says: plots ideas on a two-axis grid to find quick wins
highlights high-value, low-effort items first
flags high-effort, low-value items to drop
cards.use: want a fast visual first cut of a long list
not: multiplies four factors into a single score

cards.subject: Weighted scoring
says: rates ideas against criteria that carry agreed weights
makes the trade-off criteria explicit for stakeholders
gives a different answer when the weights change
cards.use: need to rank ideas against several business criteria that matter differently
not: classifies features by customer delight

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: estimates the value lost for each unit of time a feature is not live
distinguishes urgent items from important ones
depends on the shape of how value decays
cards.use: must choose between two features when one loses value quickly if released late
not: is the cost of the team's tools each month

cards.subject: WSJF
says: divides the cost of delay by job size
puts the item with the best delay cost per unit of effort first
is used in scaled agile frameworks to sequence work
cards.use: need to sequence jobs to minimise the total cost of delay
not: sorts features into basic, performance and delight

cards.subject: HiPPO
says: names the highest paid person's opinion winning over evidence
is countered by agreed criteria and data
creates a risk that decisions follow rank rather than customer need
cards.use: see a senior leader override a ranked list based on instinct
not: is a scoring factor for hours of effort

cards.subject: Outcome-based roadmap
says: organises plans around customer or business outcomes
leaves room to choose solutions as the team learns
avoids promising exact features and dates
cards.use: want a roadmap that states problems to solve rather than features to ship
not: lists features with fixed delivery dates

cards.subject: Now-next-later roadmap
says: groups work by how soon the team will address it
drops specific dates in favour of rough horizons
shows detail for now and increasing uncertainty for later
cards.use: need a roadmap that avoids false precision on dates
not: gives every item a committed month and quarter

cards.subject: Feature roadmap
says: lists the features planned to ship
tends to read as a promise to the audience
focuses on outputs more than outcomes
cards.use: hear stakeholders ask which features will ship next quarter
not: is organised around measurable customer outcomes

cards.subject: Date-based roadmap
says: places each item against a calendar date or quarter
creates strong expectations that turn into commitments
fits fixed external deadlines such as regulation
cards.use: must show a legal deadline that cannot move
not: uses rough horizons with no dates

cards.subject: Roadmap theme
says: groups related work under a customer problem or goal
gives several initiatives one shared purpose
reduces debates about individual features
cards.use: find a roadmap with fifty small unrelated items
not: is a single feature with its own release date

cards.subject: Objective
says: states what the team wants to achieve in a short inspiring sentence
is qualitative and is measured by key results
gives direction without naming the work
cards.use: want a short ambitious goal that people can remember
not: is a numeric target on its own

cards.subject: Key result
says: is a measurable outcome that shows an objective is met
is a result rather than a task or output
has a number and a time frame
cards.use: need a number that proves an objective was achieved
not: lists the tasks needed to finish an objective

cards.subject: Dependency mapping
says: identifies work that waits on other teams or systems
surfaces risk to dates before commitments are made
shows which roadmap items cannot start independently
cards.use: find that a planned launch waits on three other teams
not: ranks items by customer value

cards.subject: Capacity buffer
says: reserves part of the team's time for unplanned work
keeps plans honest about interruptions and bugs
avoids planning at 100 percent utilisation
cards.use: find a team always late because plans use every available hour
not: adds extra features at the end of the iteration

cards.subject: Minimum viable product
says: is the smallest version that tests a core hypothesis with real users
is built to learn rather than to impress
may be manual behind the scenes
cards.use: need the cheapest real product that tests whether customers want the core idea
not: is the final polished release with all planned features

cards.subject: Concierge MVP
says: delivers the service by hand to a few customers
proves demand before any automation is built
gives deep learning about the real workflow
cards.use: want to learn the real workflow by doing the service manually for a few customers
not: fakes an automated interface while humans work in secret

cards.subject: Wizard of Oz MVP
says: presents an automated-looking interface that people operate behind the scenes
tests how users respond before the technology exists
hides the manual work from the customer
cards.use: want to test an automated experience that is not built yet without telling users
not: tells the customer openly that staff do the work by hand

cards.subject: Fake door test
says: offers a feature that does not exist yet to measure interest
counts clicks on a call to action as a demand signal
needs a respectful message once a user clicks
cards.use: want to measure demand for a feature before building it
not: tests the usability of a built feature

cards.subject: Hypothesis
says: states a belief and the result that would prove it wrong
connects a change to an expected effect on a metric
must be falsifiable to be useful
cards.use: need a precise, testable statement before starting an experiment
not: is a confirmed fact from analytics

cards.subject: A/B test
says: compares two versions with random groups of users at the same time
isolates the effect of one change
needs enough users to detect a difference
cards.use: want to know whether a change causes better conversion
not: compares this week to last week

cards.subject: Control group
says: gets the existing experience during an experiment
provides the baseline for measuring a change
is randomly assigned to avoid bias
cards.use: need a baseline to compare the new experience against
not: is the group that receives the new variant

cards.subject: Statistical significance
says: indicates the observed difference is unlikely to be chance alone
depends on sample size and variance
does not say the effect is large or important
cards.use: see a tiny difference marked significant in a huge test and wonder whether it matters
not: proves the change will help every segment

cards.subject: Sample size
says: is the number of users needed to detect an effect reliably
should be calculated before the test starts
grows when the expected effect is smaller
cards.use: need to know how long an experiment must run before launching it
not: is chosen after seeing which variant is ahead

cards.subject: Minimum detectable effect
says: is the smallest change the test is designed to detect
sets the required sample size
is chosen from what would be worth acting on
cards.use: must decide how large a lift is worth detecting before sizing a test
not: is the largest allowed difference between groups

cards.subject: Peeking
says: is checking results repeatedly and stopping when a variant looks ahead
inflates the false positive rate
is avoided by fixing the sample size in advance
cards.use: see a team stop a test the first day the variant was ahead
not: is a design review before the test

cards.subject: Guardrail metric
says: watches for harm to something important while a primary metric is optimised
can stop a launch even if the main metric improves
covers areas such as speed, errors or cancellations
cards.use: want to make sure a conversion test does not hurt refunds or support load
not: is the single metric the experiment aims to increase

cards.subject: Novelty effect
says: inflates early engagement with a change simply because it is new
fades as users get used to the new experience
is a reason to run a test long enough to see settled behaviour
cards.use: see a new design win in week one but decline after two weeks
not: is a statistical error from small samples

cards.subject: Feature flag
says: switches a feature on or off without a new deployment
allows gradual exposure and quick rollback
separates deploying code from releasing it
cards.use: want to release a feature to ten percent of users and turn it off instantly
not: is a permanent customer setting in the product

cards.subject: Activation rate
says: measures the share of new users who reach a first meaningful value
is defined by an event that predicts later retention
moves with onboarding improvements
cards.use: want to know how many new sign-ups reach the first value
not: measures the share of customers who cancel each month

cards.subject: Retention
says: measures how many users keep coming back over time
is shown as a curve by cohort
is the strongest sign of sustained value
cards.use: need to know whether users stay after the first week
not: counts how many new users signed up

cards.subject: Churn
says: measures the share of customers lost in a period
is the complement of retention
can be tracked as users or as revenue
cards.use: want to know how many customers were lost this quarter
not: counts users who reach their first success

cards.subject: Cohort analysis
says: groups users by when they joined and follows each group over time
separates product change from the mix of new users
shows whether newer cohorts retain better
cards.use: need to know whether recent changes improved retention for new users
not: compares total users across two years

cards.subject: Funnel
says: shows the share of users who complete each step towards a goal
exposes the step with the largest drop-off
is analysed step by step in order
cards.use: need to find where users drop between sign-up and purchase
not: tracks users who return week after week

cards.subject: Conversion rate
says: is the share of visitors or users who complete a target action
can be measured for a single step or the whole funnel
has a denominator that must be defined clearly
cards.use: want a single percentage of visitors who finished the target action
not: measures how long a user stays in a session

cards.subject: Net Promoter Score
says: asks how likely users are to recommend the product on a zero to ten scale
subtracts the share of detractors from the share of promoters
ranges from minus one hundred to one hundred
cards.use: want a single loyalty indicator based on willingness to recommend
not: measures satisfaction with one support interaction

cards.subject: Customer satisfaction
says: asks how satisfied a user is with a specific interaction or feature
is collected right after the event
reflects a moment more than overall loyalty
cards.use: want a rating right after a support chat or a feature use
not: asks whether customers would recommend the company to others

cards.subject: North star metric
says: is the single measure that best captures the value delivered to customers
aligns teams toward the same outcome
should lead to long-term revenue rather than just reflect it
cards.use: need one number to align several teams around customer value
not: is the quarterly revenue target

cards.subject: Input metric
says: is a lever a team controls that drives the north star
changes sooner than the outcome it feeds
breaks the north star into parts that teams can own
cards.use: want each squad to own a number it can move that feeds the headline metric
not: is the headline measure of customer value

cards.subject: Leading indicator
says: moves early and predicts a later result
gives a team time to act before the outcome shows
is weaker as proof than the lagging result itself
cards.use: need an early signal that predicts renewal months before the contract ends
not: confirms what already happened

cards.subject: Vanity metric
says: looks impressive but does not guide a decision
grows without telling you whether users get value
includes total sign-ups and page views
cards.use: find a dashboard that only shows total registered users
not: predicts retention and informs action

cards.subject: Per-seat pricing
says: charges for each user with access
is simple to explain and predict
can discourage adding users who use the product lightly
cards.use: sell a collaboration tool where value grows with the number of team members
not: bills by the amount consumed

cards.subject: Usage-based pricing
says: charges according to consumption such as calls or storage
ties revenue closely to the value used
makes customer bills harder to predict
cards.use: sell an infrastructure service whose value scales with volume
not: charges a flat fee per user per month

cards.subject: Freemium
says: gives a free tier forever and charges for advanced use
relies on a share of free users converting to paid
costs money to serve free users
cards.use: want a large user base and expect a small share to upgrade
not: gives full access for a limited time only

cards.subject: Free trial
says: gives full or most access for a limited period
pushes users to reach value before it expires
ends in a decision to pay or leave
cards.use: want users to experience the full product before paying
not: offers a limited tier with no time limit

cards.subject: Good-better-best tiers
says: offers three packages with rising features and price
makes the middle option easy to choose
lets customers self-select by need and budget
cards.use: want to serve small and large customers with the same product
not: charges one price for all customers

cards.subject: Value-based pricing
says: sets price from the value customers gain
starts from willingness to pay and not from cost
needs customer research on the benefit received
cards.use: find that the product saves customers ten times its price yet is priced by cost
not: adds a fixed margin to cost

cards.subject: Cost-plus pricing
says: sets price by adding a margin to the cost of delivery
ignores how much value customers receive
can leave money on the table or overprice
cards.use: price a physical product from its unit cost
not: is based on what customers will pay for the benefit

cards.subject: Willingness to pay
says: is the most a customer would pay for a product
varies by segment and context
is estimated from research such as price sensitivity surveys
cards.use: need to estimate how much a segment would pay before setting a price
not: is the lowest price that covers cost

cards.subject: Grandfathering
says: keeps existing customers on an old plan when prices change
reduces churn caused by a price rise
adds support and billing complexity over time
cards.use: are raising prices and fear existing customers will leave
not: moves all customers to the new price immediately

cards.subject: Bundling
says: sells several products together at one price
raises perceived value and average order
can hide weaker components
cards.use: want to sell several features together at a single price
not: splits a product into separately priced parts

cards.subject: Onboarding
says: guides new users from sign-up to first value
reduces drop-off in the first sessions
is measured by activation
cards.use: want new users to reach first value quickly
not: handles billing disputes for existing customers

cards.subject: Aha moment
says: is the point a user first experiences the product's value
correlates with later retention
is found by comparing behaviour of retained and churned users
cards.use: want to define the moment that predicts a user will stay
not: is the first time a user logs in

cards.subject: Empty state
says: is what users see before any content exists
guides first actions instead of showing a blank screen
is a chance to teach rather than leave users stuck
cards.use: notice new users land on a blank screen and leave
not: is an error shown when a server fails

cards.subject: Product tour
says: walks users through key features with prompts
helps most when tied to a task rather than a feature list
annoys users when it blocks the screen at the start
cards.use: want to introduce interface elements in context
not: is a one-time email to new users

cards.subject: Feature adoption rate
says: is the share of eligible users who use a feature
shows whether a released feature reaches its audience
needs a clear definition of eligible users
cards.use: want to know whether a released feature gets used
not: counts the number of times a feature is mentioned in support

cards.subject: Go-to-market plan
says: coordinates product, marketing, sales and support for a launch
defines target customer, message, channels and pricing
is needed for market launches, not only code release
cards.use: need to coordinate marketing, sales and support for a launch
not: lists the technical steps to deploy code

cards.subject: Launch tiering
says: classifies launches by size to match effort and visibility
avoids treating every release as a major event
uses criteria such as customer impact and strategic value
cards.use: find the team spends the same effort on every release regardless of importance
not: groups customers into pricing plans

cards.subject: Phased rollout
says: exposes a release to a growing share of users
limits harm if a problem exists
allows monitoring before full release
cards.use: want to catch problems before every user sees a change
not: releases to everyone at once

cards.subject: Beta program
says: gives a selected group of customers early access
collects feedback before general release
works best with engaged customers who will report problems
cards.use: want feedback from willing customers before a general release
not: gradually increases traffic with no customer involvement

cards.subject: Dark launch
says: deploys a feature to production but hides it from users
tests performance under real load before exposure
separates technical risk from customer exposure
cards.use: want to test a new service under real traffic without users seeing it
not: shows the feature to a small group of customers

cards.subject: Rollback plan
says: describes how to return to the previous version if a release fails
is prepared before the launch, not during the incident
names who decides and what triggers the rollback
cards.use: are about to release a risky change and need a way back
not: lists the marketing steps for a launch

cards.subject: Product-market fit
says: exists when a product satisfies a strong market demand
shows in retention, organic growth and customers who would be upset without it
is the point after which scaling pays off more than reshaping
cards.use: need to decide if the product is ready to scale spending
not: is reached when the product has launched

cards.subject: Sean Ellis test
says: asks how users would feel if they could no longer use the product
treats a large 'very disappointed' share as a signal of fit
gives a survey-based sign of product-market fit
cards.use: want a survey signal of whether users would miss the product
not: measures the likelihood to recommend on a zero to ten scale

cards.subject: Flattening retention curve
says: levels off above zero as a cohort ages
indicates a core group of users who stay
is a quantitative sign of product-market fit
cards.use: look at a cohort chart that settles at a steady share of users
not: keeps falling towards zero over time

cards.subject: Product lifecycle
says: moves a product through introduction, growth, maturity and decline
changes what the team should prioritise at each stage
helps decide when to invest or harvest
cards.use: need to match investment to the stage a product is in
not: is the sprint cycle of the development team

cards.subject: Crossing the chasm
says: describes the gap between early adopters and the mainstream market
requires a focused niche to win first
fits technology products with a different buyer in each group
cards.use: need to move from enthusiasts to mainstream buyers who want proven solutions
not: is the gap between deployment and release

cards.subject: Sunsetting
says: retires a product or feature in a planned way
needs notice, a migration path and support
frees capacity for products with more value
cards.use: must retire an old feature that few customers use
not: deletes the feature in the next release without notice

cards.subject: Deprecation policy
says: states how long a feature stays supported after announcement
gives customers predictable time to move
applies to APIs as well as to features
cards.use: want customers to trust that features do not vanish without warning
not: lists the features planned for the next release

cards.subject: Migration path
says: gives customers a route from the old product to the new one
reduces churn during a retirement
includes tools, documentation and support
cards.use: are retiring a feature and want customers to stay
not: tells customers to find another provider

cards.subject: Sunk cost fallacy
says: continues an effort because of past spending rather than future value
makes teams keep a failing product alive
is countered by judging only future costs and benefits
cards.use: hear a team say they cannot stop because they have spent two years
not: weighs future value of the options

cards.subject: Feature bloat
says: accumulates features that make a product harder to use and maintain
comes from adding without removing
is countered by usage review and retirement
cards.use: find a product where most features are used by under one percent of users
not: describes a lean product with few features

cards.subject: Feedback loop
says: returns what customers say and do back to the team
shortens the time between a release and learning from it
needs an owner or it fills with unread input
cards.use: want every release to produce learning for the next one
not: is a one-way announcement to customers

cards.subject: Voice of the customer
says: gathers customer needs from many sources into one view
combines support, sales, research and usage data
keeps teams from relying on one loud account
cards.use: want a balanced view of customers instead of the last request heard
not: is a single survey sent once a year

cards.subject: Feedback triage
says: sorts incoming requests into themes and decides which to act on
separates the problem behind a request from the requested solution
avoids building every suggestion
cards.use: have hundreds of feature requests and no way to see patterns
not: adds every request to the roadmap in order received

cards.subject: Support tagging
says: labels support tickets by theme so patterns show up
turns support volume into product evidence
only works if tags are consistent across agents
cards.use: want support tickets to show what to fix first
not: answers customers faster with templates

cards.subject: Engineering estimate
says: is a forecast of effort with uncertainty and not a promise
improves when the team is involved in discovery
should include a range when the unknowns are large
cards.use: need to plan work and know how reliable the number is
not: is a commitment on the delivery date

cards.subject: Technical debt allocation
says: reserves a share of capacity for improving the codebase
keeps delivery speed from falling over time
needs the product manager to treat it as a priority
cards.use: find that new features slow down each quarter
not: delays all maintenance until after the next launch

cards.subject: Design critique
says: reviews a design against the user problem and goals
focuses feedback on goals rather than personal taste
includes product and engineering as well as designers
cards.use: want feedback on a design that stays on the problem
not: approves a design by seniority

cards.subject: Stakeholder alignment
says: builds shared understanding of goals and trade-offs before decisions
reduces surprises at review time
uses regular updates to show what was decided and why
cards.use: find that a launch was blocked by a leader who had not been consulted
not: gets approval from everyone for every decision

cards.subject: Decision log
says: records what was decided, by whom, why and with what alternatives
lets new people see the reasons behind past choices
prevents the same debate from reopening without new evidence
cards.use: find the team reopening a settled decision because nobody remembers why it was made
not: lists the tasks assigned in the current iteration

cards.subject: Technical spike
says: is a short time-boxed investigation of a technical unknown
answers a feasibility question rather than delivering a feature
ends with a learning, not a shippable increment
cards.use: cannot estimate a story because the integration approach is unknown
not: delivers a finished feature to customers

cards.subject: Buying committee
says: is the group of people who decide a business purchase
includes users, a champion, an economic buyer and security reviewers
makes B2B sales cycles longer than consumer ones
cards.use: sell to a large company where several roles must agree
not: is the single consumer who decides alone

cards.subject: Economic buyer
says: holds the budget and signs off on a business purchase
cares about outcomes and cost more than features
often differs from the daily user
cards.use: find that daily users love the product but the contract is not signed
not: is the person who uses the product every day

cards.subject: Champion
says: is an internal advocate who drives adoption inside a customer
helps the vendor navigate the buying process
may leave the company and take the deal with them
cards.use: need someone inside the customer to push the purchase through
not: is the person who signs the contract

cards.subject: Enterprise requirement
says: covers needs such as single sign-on, audit logs and role-based access
often blocks a deal if missing
is demanded by security and IT rather than daily users
cards.use: find that large deals stall on security questionnaires
not: is a feature loved by individual users

cards.subject: Network effect
says: makes a product more valuable as more people use it
creates a barrier for competitors
needs a critical mass before it works
cards.use: build a product whose value grows with each added user
not: makes a product cheaper to deliver at scale

cards.subject: Cold-start problem
says: is the difficulty of attracting the first users when value depends on others
is common in marketplaces and social products
is often solved by starting with one narrow segment or one side
cards.use: launch a marketplace where buyers need sellers and sellers need buyers
not: is a slow server start after a deployment

cards.subject: Platform product
says: provides capabilities that other teams or partners build on
succeeds when its customers can build without the platform team
is judged on adoption by builders
cards.use: build capabilities that many teams will use to build their own products
not: serves end users directly with a single workflow

cards.subject: API product
says: treats an interface as a product with documentation, versioning and support
has developers as customers
breaks trust when changes are made without notice
cards.use: offer an interface that outside developers integrate with
not: is hidden code inside a single application

cards.subject: Internal platform product
says: serves employees and teams as customers
gains adoption through usefulness rather than mandate
measures success by the productivity of the teams using it
cards.use: run a shared tooling team whose customers are other teams in the company
not: is sold to external customers as a subscription

qa.q: What is the difference between a problem and a solution in product work?
qa.right: A problem is a user need or pain; a solution is one way of addressing it
wrong: A problem is a bug; a solution is a release
A problem is the competitor's weakness; a solution is our feature
They are the same thing described by different teams
qa.why: Keeping the two apart lets a team consider several solutions to one problem.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of a user interview in discovery?
qa.right: To learn about the person's real behaviour, context and motivations
wrong: To get approval for the planned design
To count how many users want a feature
To ask users to pick the final solution
qa.why: Interviews give depth about why people act; they do not measure how common something is.

qa.q: What does MVP stand for in product work?
qa.right: Minimum viable product
wrong: Most valuable product
Maximum viable potential
Minimum validated process
qa.why: The MVP is the smallest product that tests the core hypothesis.

qa.q: In RICE scoring, what does the C stand for?
qa.right: Confidence
wrong: Cost
Customers
Complexity
qa.why: Confidence reduces the score of ideas that rest on weak evidence.

qa.q: What does an acceptance criterion describe?
qa.right: A testable condition that must hold for the story to be accepted
wrong: The estimated hours for the story
The person who requested the story
The release date of the story
qa.why: Acceptance criteria give a clear pass or fail.

qa.q: Which question best checks that a story is written from the user's perspective?
qa.right: What does the user get from this and why do they care?
wrong: Which database table does this touch?
How many hours will this take?
Which team owns the service?
qa.why: A user story states a need and value from the user's side.

qa.q: Which statement about the Kano model is correct?
qa.right: Features that delight today tend to become expected over time
wrong: Every feature gains value the more it is built
Basic needs delight customers when present
Delighters are the same as must-haves
qa.why: Delighters drift toward basic expectations as markets learn them.

qa.q: How is a Net Promoter Score calculated?
qa.right: Percentage of promoters minus percentage of detractors
wrong: Average of all ratings from zero to ten
Percentage of users who rated nine or ten
Number of promoters divided by detractors
qa.why: Passives are ignored and the result ranges from minus 100 to 100.

qa.q: Which roadmap format avoids committing to exact dates for later work?
qa.right: Now-next-later
wrong: Gantt chart with fixed milestones
Release calendar by month
Dependency matrix with dates
qa.why: Horizons express certainty without false precision.

qa.q: What is a north star metric?
qa.right: One measure that best captures the value customers receive
wrong: The metric the CEO prefers
The total revenue target
The number of features shipped
qa.why: It aligns teams around customer value that leads to business results.

qa.q: Which of these is a vanity metric?
qa.right: Total registered accounts ever created
wrong: Weekly retention of the latest cohort
Share of new users completing setup
Trial-to-paid conversion rate
qa.why: Cumulative totals only grow and rarely guide decisions.

qa.q: What is the difference between discovery and delivery?
qa.right: Discovery decides what is worth building; delivery builds and ships it well
wrong: Discovery is design; delivery is engineering
Discovery happens before launch; delivery after
Discovery is for new products; delivery for old ones
qa.why: Both continue throughout a product's life and involve all disciplines.

qa.q: Which pricing model charges according to how much a customer consumes?
qa.right: Usage-based
wrong: Per seat
Freemium
Tiered flat fee
qa.why: Revenue follows consumption, such as calls or storage.

qa.q: A team's A/B test shows a variant ahead after two days, and the plan was fourteen days. What should they do?
qa.right: Wait for the planned sample, because stopping early inflates false positives
wrong: Stop and ship because it is ahead
Extend to a month to be sure
Add more variants to the test
qa.why: Repeated peeking and stopping on a lead produces unreliable winners.

qa.q: Which is the best description of a guardrail metric?
qa.right: A metric that must not get worse while the main metric improves
wrong: The main metric the test aims to raise
A metric for the finance team only
A target set by the CEO for the year
qa.why: Guardrails prevent wins on one measure from hiding harm elsewhere.

qa.q: A feature request arrives from one large customer. What does product thinking suggest first?
qa.right: Understand the problem behind the request and how many others share it
wrong: Add it to the roadmap as requested
Reject it because it came from one customer
Ask engineering to estimate it before anything else
qa.why: Requests express solutions; the underlying need may be shared and solved better another way.

qa.q: What makes acceptance criteria written as Given-When-Then useful?
qa.right: They describe concrete, testable scenarios everyone can read
wrong: They remove the need for testing
They replace the user story
They set the story's priority
qa.why: Scenarios turn vague wishes into checks.

qa.q: Which activation definition is the strongest?
qa.right: An action that new users take which correlates with later retention
wrong: Logging in once
Visiting the pricing page
Opening the welcome email
qa.why: The activation event should predict long-term value, not just early activity.

qa.q: Which is a sign of product-market fit?
qa.right: Retention curves flatten and users would be very disappointed without the product
wrong: Sign-ups grow because of advertising spend
The roadmap is full for the next year
The team has shipped all planned features
qa.why: Fit shows up in sustained use and strong customer attachment.

qa.q: What is the main risk of a roadmap built as a list of features with dates?
qa.right: It reads as a promise and discourages learning and changing course
wrong: It is too short to be useful
It cannot be shared outside the team
It hides the product vision
qa.why: Date-based feature lists turn estimates into commitments.

qa.q: Why does RICE include a confidence factor?
qa.right: To lower the score of ideas whose impact is mostly a guess
wrong: To rank ideas by cost
To compare teams against each other
To show how many customers asked for the idea
qa.why: Two ideas with equal estimates differ when one has evidence.

qa.q: Which describes a concierge MVP?
qa.right: Delivering the service manually to a few customers to learn the workflow
wrong: Building a full automated product for one customer
Showing a landing page for a service that does not exist
Giving the product away for free
qa.why: The customer knows the work is manual, and the team learns before automating.

qa.q: Which pairing of research method and question is best?
qa.right: Usability test: where do users get stuck on this flow?
wrong: Survey: why did this one user abandon checkout?
Interview: how many users prefer blue?
Analytics: what do users feel about the brand?
qa.why: Each method answers a different kind of question.

qa.q: Which statement about personas is correct?
qa.right: They should be based on research and updated as understanding changes
wrong: They should be invented from team assumptions
They need a photo and a hobby to be valid
They replace talking to users
qa.why: Personas built without evidence encode bias.

qa.q: What does 'outcome over output' mean for a team?
qa.right: Success is measured by changes in user behaviour and business results, not by features shipped
wrong: Teams should ship fewer releases
Outputs are not important
Only revenue counts as an outcome
qa.why: Output is what is built; outcomes are what changes because of it.

qa.q: A team ships a redesign and overall conversion rises, but support tickets double. What is the right reading?
qa.right: The primary metric improved but a guardrail was hurt, so investigate before calling it a win
wrong: The test is a success because conversion rose
The tickets are unrelated and should be ignored
The redesign should be reverted immediately without analysis
qa.why: Success is judged on the primary metric and the harm measures together.

qa.q: A sales leader insists a custom feature is needed to close a large deal. The product manager's best first step is to
qa.right: Understand the underlying need and whether it fits the strategy and other customers
wrong: Build it to win the deal
Refuse because custom features are never acceptable
Ask engineering for a promise of a delivery date
qa.why: One deal can distort the product; test it against strategy and broader demand.

qa.q: A team has two equal-sized features and one of them loses most of its value if released after the next quarter. How should they be sequenced?
qa.right: Start with the item that loses the most value per unit of time if delayed
wrong: Start with the easiest
Start with the one the loudest stakeholder requested
Start with the most complex to reduce risk
qa.why: Cost of delay shows the urgency that raw value ranking hides.

qa.q: Your onboarding drop-off is largest at the account-connection step. What should you do first?
qa.right: Watch users at that step and find out why they stop
wrong: Add a longer welcome tutorial
Remove the step without checking
Send more reminder emails
qa.why: Identify the cause before choosing a fix.

qa.q: Which A/B test result is most trustworthy?
qa.right: One with a sample size set in advance and a single pre-registered primary metric
wrong: One that ran until the variant was significant
One that tested ten metrics and reported the best
One that compared this month to last month
qa.why: Pre-planned design avoids false positives from flexible stopping and cherry-picking.

qa.q: A new feature gets 5 percent adoption after launch. What is the most useful next step?
qa.right: Find out whether the eligible users knew it existed, tried it and why they stopped
wrong: Declare the feature a failure and remove it
Add a pop-up for all users
Ask for a larger marketing budget
qa.why: Adoption is a funnel; discover where users drop before reacting.

qa.q: Which pricing signal suggests a price rise is possible?
qa.right: Customers see strong value, churn is low and few reject the price in sales
wrong: Competitors have raised prices
The company needs more revenue
Costs have gone up
qa.why: Price follows value and demand, not the company's needs.

qa.q: A B2B product has happy users but renewals are failing. Which stakeholder has most likely been missed?
qa.right: The economic buyer who owns the budget
wrong: The newest user
The support agent
The designer
qa.why: Users alone do not decide renewal.

qa.q: An internal platform team's tool is mandated, yet teams build workarounds. What does this show?
qa.right: The platform has product gaps; adoption by mandate hides them
wrong: The teams are resisting change
The tool needs a longer training course
The mandate needs stricter enforcement
qa.why: When customers avoid a product, the product is the first place to look.

qa.q: Which is the best reason to cut a low-usage feature?
qa.right: It adds maintenance and complexity cost without value to a meaningful group, and affected users get a migration path
wrong: The competitors removed it
The team dislikes working on it
It was costly to build
qa.why: Sunset decisions rest on future costs and value, not on past spending.

qa.q: Interviewees say they would definitely pay for a new report. Usage of a similar existing report is low. What is the best interpretation?
qa.right: Stated intent is weak evidence; observed behaviour should carry more weight
wrong: The existing report needs better marketing only
The interview results are correct and should be built
The sample is too small to ignore
qa.why: Say-do gaps are common, and behaviour outranks opinion.

qa.q: A startup has strong sign-ups, retention near zero and a plan to scale marketing. What is the best advice?
qa.right: Pause scaling and fix retention first, because acquisition amplifies a leaky product
wrong: Double the marketing spend to grow faster
Add features to the roadmap
Switch the north star to sign-ups
qa.why: Without product-market fit, growth spend wastes money.

qa.q: A marketplace has many buyers but few sellers and is losing both. What approach most directly addresses the cold start?
qa.right: Focus on one narrow niche and seed supply there until it is dense
wrong: Run broad advertising to all buyers
Lower the fees for all categories
Add more features for buyers
qa.why: Marketplace value needs liquidity in a small segment first.

qa.q: A team wants to change pricing for all customers at once to a usage model. What is the safest approach?
qa.right: Test with new customers or a segment, model the effect on existing bills and consider grandfathering
wrong: Switch everyone at the next billing date
Run it only for the largest customers
Announce a change by email and wait
qa.why: Pricing changes are hard to reverse and can cause churn.

qa.q: An executive asks you to commit to feature dates for the year on the roadmap. What is the best response?
qa.right: Offer outcomes with confidence levels for near-term items and horizons for later ones
wrong: Give exact dates to avoid conflict
Refuse to share any roadmap
Share an internal engineering plan
qa.why: Honest uncertainty protects trust better than precise but false dates.

qa.q: Two teams own metrics that conflict: one raises sign-ups with free credits; the other watches revenue per user. What should leadership do?
qa.right: Agree on a shared outcome and use guardrails that both teams are measured on
wrong: Let each team optimise independently
Remove one team's metric
Pick the higher growth number
qa.why: Local metrics need a shared outcome to avoid trading away value.

qa.q: A platform product has few adopters despite good technology. Which action is most likely to help?
qa.right: Treat internal teams as customers: interview them, find the first valuable use case and support it
wrong: Mandate use by leadership
Add more features to the platform
Reduce the team
qa.why: Platforms grow through proven value for builders.

qa.q: A team keeps adding features each quarter and satisfaction is falling. Which practice would help?
qa.right: Review usage, remove or retire low-value features and define what the product will not do
wrong: Add an onboarding tour
Hire more designers
Increase release frequency
qa.why: Subtracting is part of managing complexity.

qa.q: A PM is asked to write a user story for 'build a dashboard'. What should they do first?
qa.right: Ask what decision or job the user needs the dashboard to support
wrong: Specify the charts to include
Estimate the hours needed
Assign it to a designer
qa.why: Stories should express the need, not the solution.

qa.q: Which of these is a leading indicator for subscription renewal?
qa.right: Customers' weekly use of key features in the months before renewal
wrong: Annual revenue last year
Renewal count this quarter
Total customers served to date
qa.why: Usage predicts renewal early enough to act.

qa.q: What is a good use of a feature flag during a release?
qa.right: Turning a feature on for a small share of users and off again quickly if problems appear
wrong: Locking a feature behind a higher price plan
Recording which user requested the feature
Documenting the feature for support
qa.why: Flags separate deploying code from exposing it.

qa.q: Which interview question is least likely to bias the answer?
qa.right: Tell me about the last time you did this task.
wrong: Don't you think this feature would save time?
Would you use a tool that does X?
How much would you pay for this?
qa.why: Questions about past behaviour avoid hypotheticals and leading.

qa.q: A product has 40 percent week-four retention for its newest cohort versus 25 percent a year ago, but total active users are flat. What explains it?
qa.right: Fewer new users are joining, so the cohorts improved but acquisition slowed
wrong: Retention is not improving
Older users are leaving faster
The metric is invalid
qa.why: Cohort analysis separates behaviour change from the mix of users.

qa.q: A discovery team has ten untested assumptions. Which should they test first?
qa.right: The one with the highest impact if wrong and the least evidence
wrong: The easiest to test
The one the CEO believes
The one the team is most confident in
qa.why: Risk is impact times uncertainty.

qa.q: A retired API is still used by a few large customers. What is the most appropriate action?
qa.right: Give a dated notice, provide a migration route and support, then retire as announced
wrong: Remove it quietly in the next release
Keep it forever
Tell customers to rewrite their integrations by themselves
qa.why: Predictable retirement preserves trust.

qa.q: During planning, engineering says a story cannot be estimated. What should the team do?
qa.right: Time-box a spike to resolve the unknown and then estimate
wrong: Estimate it as large
Skip the story
Estimate it based on the last similar story
qa.why: Spikes convert unknowns into estimable work.
